reps.md:
Athens is a 19th-century capital built on top of an ancient city, and then flooded with people in the 20th. Most of what this map shows sits in the gaps between those layers.

## Layers

**Ancient (to about 500).** The Acropolis, the Agora, Kerameikos and the hills around them (Areopagus, Pnyx, Philopappou) are the old core. Two rivers, the Eridanos and the Ilisos, ran through it; both are buried now.

**Byzantine and Ottoman (500–1833).** Athens was a small town. Its churches were built from the ruins of temples, and the Ottomans added mosques, a medrese and fountains. Few survived the next step.

**The Bavarian capital (1834–1922).** King Otto made Athens the capital and his architects (Klenze, Hansen, Ziller, Kaftanzoglou) laid out a neoclassical city, demolishing many old churches on the way.

**Refugees and modernism (1922–1940).** After 1922 over a million refugees came from Asia Minor; whole suburbs (Nea Smyrni, Kokkinia, Kaisariani, Nea Ionia) were built for them, and the first modern apartment blocks went up in Kypseli and Exarchia.

**War, occupation, civil war (1940–1949).** The Occupation, the famine, the Dekemvriana and the Civil War left precise marks: cells, walls, plaques.

**The polykatoikia city (1950–).** The postwar boom turned Athens into the white sea of apartment blocks you see from Lycabettus. The junta (1967–74), the 2004 Olympics and the crisis of the 2010s added their own ruins.

## Bearings

The Acropolis is the centre. Syntagma lies east of it, Omonia north, Piraeus 8 km south-west. Lycabettus is the high hill to the north-east; Hymettus, Penteli and Parnitha close the basin on three sides, the sea on the fourth.

## What this map is for

Not the postcard: the curves of the Parthenon's steps rather than the view, the Kommandantur cells rather than the changing of the guard, the concrete and the ruins rather than the souvenir streets. The classics are here too, each with one detail to find.

Athens has two great concrete stories and one great ruin story.

**The 1930s.** Kypseli's Fokionos Negri, Exarchia's Blue Building and the Prosfygika on Alexandras are some of the best interwar modernism in Europe, built fast for a city that had just doubled in size.

**The modernists.** Pikionis made one modernist school and turned away to lay the Philopappou paths. Zenetos designed a round school, a theatre in a quarry and an 'electronic' city that was never built. Konstantinidis built bare concrete frames for workers and for the Xenia hotels.

**The ruins.** The mountains hold 1930s sanatoria and Cold War missile and radar sites; the coast holds the 2004 Olympic venues and the industrial belt of Piraeus. Some are going fast: Hellinikon is now a park, the Faliro stadium is next.

Start with: the Prosfygika, Zenetos's round school, the Papadimitriou sanatorium (from outside), Lipasmata park.

The small sights of Athens are mostly about the 1940s and the junta, and about water.

- **Cells and walls.** Korai 4 keeps prisoners' graffiti 6 m underground; the Kokkinia Mantra keeps ricochet marks; Kaisariani's wall saw the 200 shot on 1 May 1944.
- **The junta.** Bouboulinas 18 is gone, Mesogeion 14–18 keeps two cells, the Polytechnic keeps its crushed gate.
- **Water.** The Eridanos still runs under Monastiraki station; the Ilisos shows itself for a few metres at Agia Fotini; one Ottoman fountain survives, a metre below the road.
- **Odd objects.** A medrese gate with a tulip, a little column that named a district, the last guillotine in a medical school.

Start with: Korai 4, Monastiraki station, the open Ilisos.

Otto's planners demolished dozens of Byzantine churches to make the new capital, so every old church in central Athens is a survivor, wedged between shops and offices. The ones on this map are the oddest: a column through a roof, a church built of 90 older carvings, a chapel under a ministry on stilts, a cave church on Lycabettus, a rock chapel in the Parthenon's quarry.

The 19th century adds the Catholic cathedral with its spare palace columns, the 20th a Bauhaus-era Protestant church and Pikionis's re-clad chapel, and 2020 the city's first official mosque. The cemeteries are among the best stops: the First Cemetery's marble, the sea-facing Phaleron War Cemetery and the German crypts at Dionysos.

Start with: Routes › Tours by topic › Church hunt through the ages.

**No combined ticket.** It was abolished in 2024. Each site charges separately. Acropolis €30 (reduced €15); one 2026 guide gives Agora €20, Olympieion €20, Roman Agora and Hadrian's Library €10, Kerameikos €10, Lyceum €5. Check hh.gr; prices change.

**Hours.** Acropolis in winter 8:00–17:00; the Agora 8:00–19:30 from April 2026 (shorter in winter); small sites often 8:00–15:00 in winter. Free entry on the 1st and 3rd Sunday from November to March and on a few national days.

**Book.** Acropolis timed tickets online; Newall telescope and Thissio Observatory evening shows; the Criminology Museum by appointment (good luck).

**Dates that decide a stop.** Omorfokklisia opens only on St George's day. Lycabettus Theatre only for summer concerts. Tatoi's museums were due to open in December 2026. The Polytechnic closes around 17 November.

Manual follow-up on the threads of the five discovery runs (D1, D2, D3, R1, K1) and the master report (M). ~45 searches/fetches. Priority: time-sensitive states first (openings, closures, demolitions), then the strongest open leads, then a catalogue sweep. Results are merged into `athens/athens-sites.md` (register). No Google pins this round.

**Catalogue sweep — mostly blocked.** listedmonuments.culture.gr refuses automated fetching (robots); the TEE culture2000 register pages carry no index link; the USI/Sergison "Athens Survey" PDF (2025, a numbered list of 1950s–60s polykatoikies with addresses) failed to load — only part of its list came through in search snippets (used below). Next time: open these three by hand in a browser.

## 1. Time-sensitive states

- **Kerameikos** — was closed for the 2023–26 upgrade; **reopened 15 Sept 2026** (To Vima English, inauguration with the minister). K1's practical lines are superseded. Source: tovima.com "Reopened Kerameikos site".
- **Ancient Agora** — hours 08:00–19:30 from 1 Apr 2026 "until further notice" (hh.gr notice, 2 Apr 2026). Winter hours from 1 Nov not found; check hh.gr before going.
- **Site prices after the combined ticket** — one 2026 guide gives Agora €20, Olympieion €20, Roman Agora €10, Hadrian's Library €10, Kerameikos €10, Lyceum €5 (Acropolis €30). Secondary source, not checked against hh.gr; treat as indicative.
- **Tatoi** (M A10) — historic core due "late 2026"; Greek City Times (3 Oct 2026) reports a December opening. Still a works site as of this pass. Check in December.
- **Hellinikon** (M A1) — the Saarinen terminal, control tower, listed hangars, runway and canoe-kayak facilities are kept as elements of the new park (Protothema, June 2026); the Sports Park opened in stages from **20 July 2026** (Ta Nea / To Vima). The "abandoned" layer is effectively gone: reframe the stop as airport relics inside a new park.
- **Faliro beach volleyball** (M A2) — still derelict in AFP photos (Feb 2024); the Aenaon Park plan turns it into an open-air events amphitheatre; the neighbouring Tae Kwon Do hall was conceded to the Attica Region for 40 years from 1 Jan 2026 (2026–27 = studies). See it soon; exterior only.
- **Mouria** (M C3, D3) — conflict resolved as far as possible: in July 2026 the owner's daughter said the corner **stays a café, "we don't know if it will be Mouria"** (LiFO 7 Jul; aftodioikisi 8 Jul). D3 reports Mouria itself closed 31 Oct 2026. Verdict: Mouria as such probably gone; the corner remains a café. Downgrade to extra; check on site.
- **Vallianeio reading room** (D3) — reopening announced "within 2026" (parapolitika); no confirmation that it happened. Unresolved.
- **Hellenic Conservatory, Feidiou 3** (D3) — €5.7m restoration (Culture Ministry); listed among the 2026 openings (To Vima, Jan 2026) as the future Dance Archive. Not confirmed open.
- **Demokritos reactor** (D3) — no longer operating (cnn.gr); no museum or open day found. Extra only.
- **Keratsini "Agios Georgios" power station** (D1) — efsyn/Parliament: produced power 1928–2012. VI.D.A.'s "reserve units 8–9" refers to the later gas units. A 2023 Environment Ministry decision **listed the historic buildings, façades and the red-and-white chimney**. Use: historic plant closed 2012, listed 2023.
- **Kaisariani range memorial** (M B3) — vandalised in Feb 2026, hours after the release of the rediscovered photos of the 200 (Greek City Times); municipality promised repairs.
- **Goudi "Badminton" theatre** — fire on 12 July 2026 (Protothema headline). Not researched further; a possible addition to the Olympic-venues layer.

## 2. Verdicts on threads

### Concrete, Cold War, industry (D1)
- **Zenetos's Kavouri house** (Derechani 32, not "Decherani") — **destroyed**, according to NTUA professor Dimitris Papalexopoulos (USModernist). Drop.
- **NIKE batteries** (thread 1) — the Air Force history confirms the 1960 squadron with four flights at **Keratea, Hymettus, Parnitha and Kithairon** (parapolitika quoting haf.gr). The exact Hymettus and Parnitha sites were not found. The US Nike Historical Society has sketches by a US "D team" (558th Artillery Group, the custody detachment for the warheads) attached to the Greek 350th Nike Group in 1969–70 — a good guide-text detail. Keratea stays the only physical stop.
- **Penteli NATO station** (thread 2) — nothing new; ACE High is the likely network name. Unresolved.
- **Ardittos shelter** (thread 4) — the largest in Attica, ~1,300 people (Skai). Build date conflict: Skai says built by the Germans 1943–44; parapolitika/in.gr say prewar, requisitioned. Three of its four entrances are sealed, one remains. Exact entrance not found.
- **New: Lycabettus shelter** — c. 1936, next to the Agioi Isidoroi cave church, runs ~100 m into the rock, two entrances, larger and better preserved than Ardittos (parapolitika, in.gr, aftodioikisi 2026). Pairs with Agioi Isidoroi (R1). Closed.
- **Keratsini closure date** (thread 5) — resolved above (2012).
- **Valsamakis, Semitelou 5** (D1 #8) — confirmed: Valsamakis's first building, near Plateia Mavili; he himself sent photos of it under construction (parianostypos). Upgrade to CONFIRMED.
- **Rentis OEK blocks, Konstantinidis Xenia near Athens, Doxiadis, Dekeleia, Kalogreza, Hadrian's aqueduct shafts, Moschato/Tavros factories, Schinias/Agios Kosmas, Salamina bunkers, Alimos bunkers, Kypseli shelter access** — not reached. Remain open.

### Pass-by (D2)
- **Mesogeion 14–18** (thread 3) — Protothema (Nov 2025) confirms the Security Police moved here from Bouboulinas 18 in 1971; Bouboulinas 18 was demolished shortly before the junta fell (a block of flats now). The Mesogeion building dates from 1960 and has ~18 owners (Retrieving Athens, Univ. of Patras). Whether the cells open on 17 Nov: unresolved.
- **Agia Dynami** (D2/R1) — the building that swallowed it is Patroklos Karantinos's old Ministry of Education (1950s); the ministry left in 2007 and the block has stood empty since (efsyn, vimaorthodoxias). A **tunnel from the church to the Ilisos near Kallirroi** is reported — treat as legend. The 15 m munitions chamber stays unresolved (Agia Dynami vs Russian Church).
- **Loumbarda monument, kilometre zero, noon time-ball, Thrasyllos sundial, Perama tram rails, Lavrio rails (lavriaki 4 Nov), guillotine site, toilets, Faros wall** — searched or not reached; no new evidence. Remain LEADs.

### Thinkers and science (D3)
- **Old Chemistry, Solonos 104** — confirmed open: Law School Library Mon–Fri 8:30–20:00 (law.lib.uoa.gr). **New:** the building also houses the **University's Museum of Natural Sciences and Technology** — over 10,000 scientific instruments, including a Telefunken telegraphy collection and the archive of the University of Smyrna that Carathéodory saved; at the foundation ceremony (6 June 1887) a glass cylinder with a gold coin and a dedication was laid in the foundations (en.uoa.gr). Strong fit; visits via the museum contact (chsymeon@phys.uoa.gr).
- **Weights-and-measures prototypes** (thread 2) — no evidence found that Greece's national metre/kilogram copies were kept here. The 1978 decree defines Greek units by the Sèvres prototypes. Keep only as an unproven story line.
- **Finos Film** (thread 5) — Chiou 53 confirmed (Wikipedia; ~500 reels rescued from the building in July 2021, cnn.gr). The 1958 studios at Agioi Anargyroi were **the former stables of Ioannis Merlas, in the Mykoniatika area** — this settles the "Kalleri vs Merlas" conflict towards Merlas. **Atlantis** (D3 #42) located: Thymarakia, Liosion St, beside the old Atlantis cement factory.
- **Spilia tou Paraskeva / Never on Sunday** (thread 1) — no source places a scene there. Unresolved; keep the film link out of the guide text.
- **Mouria, Vallianeio, Conservatory, reactor** — see section 1.

### Religious (R1)
- **Omorfokklisia** — confirmed: **opens only once a year, on St George's feast** (Easter Monday in 2024; Protothema, Orthodoxia News Agency). Coordinates fixed from en.wikipedia: 38.0289, 23.7638 (Galatsi). Plan the visit for that day or treat as an exterior stop.
- **Agios Ioannis tis Kolonas** — access conflict: a 2013 church blog gives mornings 08:30–13:00, closed Sundays; Atlas Obscura says it is a chapel of Agios Dimitrios with a liturgy once a month. The courtyard and column are visible from Evripidou either way. Date: a single-aisled basilica of 565 (blog) / "6th century" (Spotted by Locals). Atlas Obscura's claim that the Eridanos runs audibly under the church = LEAD.
- **Davelis cave** — walkable (hiking reports, Apr 2026). **Correction:** Wikipedia says there is no evidence of Pan worship in this cave; the Pan and nymphs shrine is a smaller cave ~800 m up the slope to the NE (excavated 1952, finds in the National Archaeological Museum). The ancient sledge path for the marble is partly preserved.
- **Ano Glyfada church (Molfesis & Papagiannis)** — still only "design, 1961" (ek-mag essay); built form unknown. Unresolved.
- **New lead from the same essay:** **Giannakis's Air Force chapel on the summit of Mt Kithairon (1960)**, built during his military service — "almost anti-plastic" massing. Day trip; near the old Kithairon NIKE flight.
- **15 m chamber, Eileithyia under the Little Metropolis, Catholic/Armenian cemeteries, refugee churches** — not reached.

### Classics (K1)
- **Kerameikos and Agora hours** — see section 1. **Byron graffito position, 1687 shell fragment, Ottoman ship graffiti, stadium herms, Eleusis bust, North Slope winter hours** — not resolved this round.

## 3. Gap-fill finds (new to the register)
- **Zenetos & Apostolidis, Amalias 34 / Daidalou** (1959–60) — the block with sliding façade panels later copied badly all over Athens (archetype.gr; USI survey). Standing.
- **Postwar polykatoikies from the USI "Athens Survey" (2025)**, partial list: Valsamakis, Vas. Sofias 129 (1955–56); Valsamakis, Irodotou 17 (1955–56); Valsamakis, Vas. Konstantinou 42 / Pl. Proskopon (1959–60); Molfesis, Vas. Konstantinou 46 (1959); Papazisis, Mithimnis 34 / Patision (1957–58); Antonakakis & Gartzos, Argolidos 26 (1961–62).
- **Vourekas, Zolotas house, Dionysiou Areopagitou 27** (completed 1960) — austere modernist house facing the Acropolis (To Vima).
- **Athens Hilton** — Vasileiadis, Vourekas & Staikos, 1959–63; foundation stone Feb 1959 with Karamanlis (LiFO). D1 thread 9 partly answered.
- **Sotiria hospital** — 1936 buildings by Periklis Georgakopoulos and Ioannis Despotopoulos (Laiko hospital and the kitchens/laundry/dormitory block), listed in a 2016 survey of key modern works (UCL/Giamarelos). LEAD: which buildings stand unaltered.
- **Lycabettus shelter** and **Natural Sciences & Technology Museum** — see above.
